name: Nationalism
summary: Nationalism holds that nations are real and valuable communities, that their members owe one another special duties, and that each nation may claim to govern itself, ideally in a state matching it. Its thinkers differ on what makes a nation (shared will and memory for Renan, language for Fichte, a divine design for Mazzini) and on how far the nation's claims reach beyond self-rule.
scope: Doctrine of the nation only: national identity, territory, self-determination, language, culture and the means. The core is Mazzini's Duties of Man, Renan's What is a Nation?, Mill's chapter on nationality, Fichte's Addresses, Wilson's Fourteen Points and the Stanford scholarship on Herder and nationalism. The programme of any party or government that carried a nationalism (economics, welfare, social policy, general foreign policy) is excluded as borrowing, as is the economic nationalism of tariffs and self-sufficiency.

missingStatements.text: Members of a nation owe special duties to their compatriots that they do not owe to humanity at large.
missingStatements.rationale: The Stanford entry names special duties to compatriots as one of the three beliefs shared by all forms of nationalism, and Mazzini calls the country a family we sympathise with more readily than others.

missingStatements.text: A nation rests on a shared memory of its past.
missingStatements.rationale: Renan makes a rich legacy of memories one of two constituents of the nation and Mill calls the community of recollections the strongest cause of national feeling.

notes: Themes searched in the sources read: nation and identity, self-determination, territory and boundaries, language, culture and education, minorities, race and religion as criteria, colonialism and conquest, the means. Economy, welfare, social policy and most government themes are null because the texts are silent or a party programme would be borrowing. Strands that conflict (Renan's consent against Fichte's language, liberal against conservative, Herder and Mazzini against Mill on other peoples) are recorded as splits. The Mazzini chapters other than I and V, Herder's own text and the books of Gellner, Anderson and Smith could not be read.
